frozen_original.title: Birthright Citizenship Executive Order Blocked by Four Courts
frozen_original.synopsis: On January 20, 2025, Trump signed an executive order directing federal agencies to refuse to recognize U.S. citizenship for children born on U.S. soil if neither parent is a citizen or lawful permanent resident — a direct challenge to the 14th Amendment's citizenship clause, settled law since United States v. Wong Kim Ark (1898). Federal judges blocked the order within days; three separate courts issued nationwide injunctions in early 2025. The 9th Circuit ruled the order unconstitutional on July 23, 2025, and the 1st Circuit upheld a nationwide injunction on October 3, 2025. The Supreme Court's June 27, 2025 ruling limiting 'universal injunctions' complicated enforcement of the blocks without overturning them, leaving the order universally suspended as of August 2026.

frozen_original.title: Iran Retaliates with Ballistic Missiles at US Bases in Middle East
frozen_original.synopsis: Within 48 hours of the US-Israeli airstrikes on its nuclear facilities, Iran launched salvos of ballistic missiles targeting US military installations across the Middle East in June 2025. The strikes hit bases in Iraq, Qatar, and the UAE, injuring dozens of US service members and killing at least three. Iran used its Shahab-3 and Emad medium-range ballistic missiles, which US and allied missile defense systems only partially intercepted. The retaliatory strikes forced the evacuation of non-essential personnel from several bases and triggered emergency calls between Trump and allied leaders. The episode demonstrated that the military strikes on Iran's nuclear facilities had not eliminated Iran's conventional military capability to threaten US forces.

frozen_original.title: Bondi DOJ Drops Antitrust Case Against Google After Major Trump Donor Receives Benefit
frozen_original.synopsis: In March 2025, Attorney General Pam Bondi's Justice Department abruptly dropped a major antitrust case against Google that the Biden DOJ had been pursuing in federal court after establishing through extensive litigation that Google had illegally monopolized the online advertising market — a case described by antitrust lawyers as one of the most significant competition enforcement actions in decades. The dismissal came after Google's parent company Alphabet made substantial financial commitments to Trump-aligned causes and after Google CEO Sundar Pichai attended meetings with Trump at Mar-a-Lago and the White House. Ethics watchdogs filed formal complaints alleging the dismissal represented a quid pro quo — law enforcement used as a commodity traded for political support and financial benefit. The episode was described as the most blatant example of pay-to-play federal prosecution since the Gilded Age.

primary.title: DOJ Drops Proposed Google AI-Investment Divestiture While Seeking Other Remedies
primary.description_short: DOJ revised its Google search-case proposal on March 7, 2025, dropping mandatory AI-investment divestiture while retaining a proposed Chrome divestiture.
primary.description_medium: On March 7, 2025, the Justice Department filed a revised proposed judgment in the Google search-monopoly case. The proposal dropped mandatory divestiture of Google's AI investments in favor of advance notice for future investments, while retaining a proposed Chrome divestiture and other remedies. Reuters reported that DOJ and 38 state attorneys general continued seeking court relief. This was a change in proposed remedies, not dismissal of the antitrust case or a final court order.
primary.description_long: On March 7, 2025, the U.S. Department of Justice and plaintiff states filed a revised proposed final judgment in the federal search-monopoly case against Google. The filing changed the remedies sought: plaintiffs stopped seeking mandatory divestiture of Google's AI investments and instead proposed prior notification of future investments. It maintained other central requests, including Google's divestiture of Chrome, restrictions on search-related payments to distribution partners, and data-sharing provisions. Reuters reported that DOJ and a coalition of 38 state attorneys general still sought a court order requiring Chrome's sale and other measures. The filing was a proposal submitted for the court's consideration; it did not dismiss the antitrust case or establish a quid pro quo. The supplied record's claim that Attorney General Pam Bondi dropped the case after Alphabet made political contributions or held meetings with Donald Trump is not supported by the accessed sources and is excluded. The official filing says plaintiffs changed the AI remedy after additional discovery, but this alone does not prove the rationale or rule out other motives. This corrected entry is limited to the documented procedural change and the remedies still proposed at that point.
primary.subcategory: Proposed remedies in the Google search case

corrected_proposal.title: DOJ Drops Proposed Google AI-Investment Divestiture While Seeking Other Remedies
corrected_proposal.description_short: DOJ revised its Google search-case proposal on March 7, 2025, dropping mandatory AI-investment divestiture while retaining a proposed Chrome divestiture.
corrected_proposal.description_medium: On March 7, 2025, the Justice Department filed a revised proposed judgment in the Google search-monopoly case. The proposal dropped mandatory divestiture of Google's AI investments in favor of advance notice for future investments, while retaining a proposed Chrome divestiture and other remedies. Reuters reported that DOJ and 38 state attorneys general continued seeking court relief. This was a change in proposed remedies, not dismissal of the antitrust case or a final court order.
corrected_proposal.description_long: On March 7, 2025, the U.S. Department of Justice and plaintiff states filed a revised proposed final judgment in the federal search-monopoly case against Google. The filing changed the remedies sought: plaintiffs stopped seeking mandatory divestiture of Google's AI investments and instead proposed prior notification of future investments. It maintained other central requests, including Google's divestiture of Chrome, restrictions on search-related payments to distribution partners, and data-sharing provisions. Reuters reported that DOJ and a coalition of 38 state attorneys general still sought a court order requiring Chrome's sale and other measures. The filing was a proposal submitted for the court's consideration; it did not dismiss the antitrust case or establish a quid pro quo. The supplied record's claim that Attorney General Pam Bondi dropped the case after Alphabet made political contributions or held meetings with Donald Trump is not supported by the accessed sources and is excluded. The official filing says plaintiffs changed the AI remedy after additional discovery, but this alone does not prove the rationale or rule out other motives. This corrected entry is limited to the documented procedural change and the remedies still proposed at that point.
corrected_proposal.subcategory: Proposed remedies in the Google search case
